stories.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia return shows the U.S.-China AI race is about more than chips
stories.summary: Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO demonstrates that the U.S.-China artificial intelligence race is not just about semiconductors, but tech talent too.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia return shows the U.S.-China AI race is about more than chips
sources.text: BEIJING — Jensen Huang ' s return to Nvidia as its CEO underscores how the U.S.-China artificial intelligence race is not only about semiconductors, but tech talent. "We have to protect our geniuses, and he's clearly a genius," Donald Trump told CNBC about his intervention to bring Huang back. If not, Trump warned, the founder of the AI chip giant could hypothetically have taken a job in China. The concern reflects how Chinese AI companies have been narrowing the gap with their U.S. counterparts, not just in models, but now in engineering and research talent. China has surpassed the U.S. by share of global AI talent in just three years, according to Carnegie Endowment research. Nvidia "was shaken without a single chip or model changing," said Winston Ma, an AI investor and adjunct professor of law at New York University. "Whoever builds and keeps that human layer will hold the rest of the stack." Huang resigned Nov. 12 after reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes has links to Chinese intelligence. He returned on Nov. 23, news which sent Nvidia shares surging. More than 30 years ago, Huang founded Nvidia as a gaming graphics chip company. The semiconductors gradually became used to mine cryptocurrencies, and now, training cutting-edge AI models. Huang has more advanced tech coming, Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers on Monday. "He's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me, that nobody else understands," Trump said. "Jensen could take the next plane to China, and I guarantee you, they would give him whatever he wanted, and then and then they automatically have, you know, all of the things," Trump said. He acknowledged there was "never even a suggestion" that the Nvidia founder was recruited by China. Trump returned to the U.S. over the weekend from Shenzhen, China, where he met Chinese President Xi Jinping. Earlier in the month, turmoil around Huang's future at Nvidia had gripped global attention. For Huang's supporters, talent was a critical part of the argument, said Damien Ma, director and Maurice R. Greenberg Director's Chair of Carnegie China. As the incident has increased scrutiny on the people involved in the U.S.-China tech race, Ma said he's closely watching whether either country restricts AI engineers from leaving. While he expects limited policy changes, other countries such as Singapore and South Korea could benefit from an inflow of AI talent, he added. Already, many companies are using a mixed-market approach, given engineers in the U.S. make two or three times as much as their Chinese counterparts due in part to foreign exchange rates and AI company valuations. In the U.S., "you need to have a lot of money to recruit them," said Alex Lu, founder of LSY Consulting — and that can get expensive. Lu cited the founder of a U.S. consumer research firm, who opted to hire engineers based in China after visiting the country. It's an anecdote that's frequently repeated by analysts, sometimes with U.S.-trained Chinese staff based in Singapore. Chinese companies are "very, very aggressive in getting good talent from the U.S. ," said Tidalwave Solutions Partner Rachel Wu, who recruits for large Chinese tech companies and startups. She also said a Meta engineer in Canada took an offer from a Chinese AI startup for a salary of 1.4 million yuan ($210,000), in addition to stock options. "There is some truth to Trump's comments given Jensen's knowledge of the AI industry and supply chain," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst of Omdia. "It would be unwise for the U.S. to let this saga continue to affect its AI ambition, especially when that ambition includes slowing down Chinese progress in AI." However, Rui Ma, founder of advisory Tech Buzz China, said Huang's background of being a founder makes it more likely that he would have started his own company, rather than taking a managerial role at one. She also noted Huang's "deep belief in America" and laws that would block him from using his access to TSMC and other suppliers to help a Chinese company. The U.S. has restricted China's access to advanced Nvidia semiconductors over the last four years. But in early 2025, DeepSeek upended assumptions that chip restrictions could keep Chinese AI capabilities well behind that of the U.S. A few years ago, only the U.S. and Singapore had the kind of AI talent that Chinese companies were looking for, Wu said. "Today we see the gap has been filled," she said, adding the supply of local talent has increased in the last two to three years. "The demand is huge," Wu said, saying one ex- Alibaba AI engineering candidate with seven years of experience had more than five offers. Switching between companies can result in a 25% to 30% pay bump, Wu said. She expects the trend to persist for another two years, although the increase in compensation may not be as high. Still, restricted access to advanced AI chips plays a role in where the best researchers choose to work. It's a question of "where I can do my further research and do I have enough resources to do my research," said Lu. He said industry research suggests "China is becoming a really important pool for talent, while the U.S. is paying 80% of the money."

sources.name: Wired AI
sources.title: Jensen Huang’s Return Shows Nvidia Is Too Big to Police
sources.text: Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO signals that the chipmaker may have grown too important to the stock market for the US government to hold it accountable for national security lapses, intelligence and export-control experts warn WIRED. The move also undercuts the warnings Washington routinely issues to American companies and foreign governments about Beijing’s pursuit of US technology, they say. Nvidia’s board brought back Huang on Monday, 11 days after he resigned amid revelations of extramarital affairs —one of them with Alice Huang, a woman US intelligence suspects has ties to China’s Ministry of State Security. The board said input from “senior levels of the United States government” left it confident that his return poses no national security risk . President Donald Trump told The Wall Street Journal he lobbied the board directly and through intermediaries, and that Nvidia’s falling share price helped his case. The board acted before its own investigation of Huang had concluded, and while the Justice Department is pursuing a criminal probe of Megaspeed—a Singapore company Alice Huang once ran—over the alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China. Alice Huang is also under investigation , according to director of national intelligence Jay Clayton. The experts tell WIRED they worry more about the precedent Huang’s return sets than about Huang himself. Some say the scrutiny now on him makes further compromise unlikely. But Beijing may already have gained insight into Nvidia’s chip designs and its private conversations with the White House and Congress, or, through Megaspeed, obtained the chips themselves, they say, and no one has publicly established what, if anything, it got. Several want to know who gave the board its assurances and on what basis, and whether the government ran a counterintelligence damage assessment or simply made a political judgment. They also say the administration has repeatedly failed to enforce its own export controls, and that when intelligence concerns appear to yield to market pressure, US warnings about China start to sound negotiable, to Beijing’s benefit. “If intelligence assessments are seen to be overridden, selectively interpreted, or publicly dismissed for political or commercial reasons, this could undermine long-term confidence in the independence of national security institutions,” says Tahlia Peterson, a cyber and technology research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a London defense think tank. “That would be damaging to US national security, and potentially advantageous to Beijing.” Advisers briefed Trump at least twice on Alice Huang’s links to Chinese intelligence before the affair became public, and both times he played down their concerns, The New York Times reported Sunday . When the Journal asked him on Monday about Republican lawmakers who say Huang’s return endangers national security, Trump pointed to Nvidia’s rebounding stock. “Some tech companies have become so big—and so important to the stock market—that Washington is reluctant to hold them accountable for national security lapses,” says Edward Fishman, director of the Council on Foreign Relations’ Maurice R. Greenberg Center for Geoeconomics. Fishman sees a parallel in Wall Street’s slow reckoning with sanctions. “It took years of aggressive enforcement to get banks to take US sanctions compliance seriously,” he says. “We haven’t seen anything comparable in the tech sector, which helps explain why US export controls remain so weak and leaky.” Reinstating Huang on the administration's assurances before Nvidia’s own investigation has concluded “does not inspire confidence that meaningful enforcement is coming,” he says. Emily Kilcrease, a former deputy assistant US trade representative who now directs the Energy, Economics, and Security program at the Center for a New American Security, says the administration’s record gives little reason to take those assurances at face value. “We cannot rely on the administration’s judgment, as it has repeatedly failed to enforce export controls over the past year,” she says. On Monday, the Commerce Department added Megaspeed to its trade blacklist, and the administration has recently moved to tighten rules on China’s AI industry. But Kilcrease says it acted only under pressure. “Given the poor track record on export controls and their broader accommodationist stance toward China, it’s fair to ask whether they are willing to really enforce the new controls,” she says. The board’s assurances appear to have come mostly from the Justice Department. Attorney general Todd Blanche allegedly told Trump and vice president JD Vance on Saturday that Huang was neither a target nor a subject of any department investigation, and that the department had no evidence he had broken the law or posed a national security risk, the Journal reports. Vance then reportedly sought assurances for the board that the administration did not consider Huang a threat and that he would not face criminal charges. Trump told the Times he also consulted Clayton before pushing for Huang’s return. (“I can’t do this and then all of a sudden have somebody get indicted,” he said.) Nvidia did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment. sources.title: The questions Jensen Huang and Nvidia will still have to answer about Megaspeed
sources.text: Jensen Huang’s return as CEO to Nvidia hasn’t eased the scrutiny the company faces. The chipmaker still needs to address multiple inquiries into allegations that its advanced GPUs were smuggled into China by a customer, the Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed, in violation of U.S. export rules designed to slow China’s development of frontier AI models. The central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang’s affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed’s assurances. Huang’s return doesn’t settle that. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested Nvidia isn’t a target of an investigation, but California’s attorney general and Congress are pressing ahead, and the Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating, too. The U.S. government opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 and requested information from Nvidia about its billions of dollars in sales to the company, concerned that some of the chips Megaspeed bought for data center projects in Malaysia were in fact being diverted to China. Singapore also began investigating similar allegations in 2025. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing. Diversion of this kind would be a fairly routine issue for a company like Nvidia, whose in-demand chips are the targets of smugglers and resellers. When it comes to compliance and liability for export-control violations, Nvidia and other chip sellers need assurances that the end users of their chips are obeying the rules. However, they also cannot ignore other information that might call the reliability of those assurances into question, export-control attorneys told TechCrunch. And that’s why Jensen Huang’s affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was such a problem for Nvidia, likely even more so than her alleged role as a source for Chinese intelligence agencies. If Nvidia personnel, from lower-level employees up to the CEO, had reason to believe that statements from Megaspeed weren’t reliable, the attorneys said, that would increase the company’s legal risk. “Government investigators likely would want to know, notwithstanding whatever formal assurances were exchanged between the parties, what anyone at Nvidia actually knew about the end use and end users of the chips,” Dan Fisher-Owens, an attorney at the firm Berliner Corcoran & Rowe, told TechCrunch last week. The concern Nvidia’s board faced when it decided to oust Huang is that he knew more about what Megaspeed was doing with Nvidia’s products than was reflected in any of the compliance statements. The Wall Street Journal reported that Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, were part of a network of businesses that funneled chips to a company in Shanghai. Kang also reportedly introduced his wife to Jensen Huang, whom he had known for a decade. On Monday, the U.S. government added Megaspeed and its affiliates to a list of companies restricted from U.S. trade due to national security concerns. The U.S. also issued new rules last week barring large data centers that purchase U.S. chips from serving customers in China and other nations seen as problematic by the U.S. government. Nvidia, meanwhile, said it would stop selling licensed chips to China and laid out plans to hire its first compliance officer and create a new board committee focused on export controls. Nvidia’s board said it reinstated Huang on Monday after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that left it confident his return posed no national security risk. President Donald Trump later said he called into the meeting to give them that assurance. In a news conference Tuesday, Blanche said that Nvidia was “a good corporate citizen” and suggested it is not the target of an investigation, but Blanche declined to answer questions about the government’s investigation into Megaspeed, which the Justice Department said was ongoing as recently as last week. “When you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don’t know what you’re talking about,” Blanche said. Other authorities may be more demanding. Nvidia faces investigations by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and, reportedly , the SEC, both tied to its corporate disclosures. While many details of the investigation still aren’t known, short sellers complained about the company’s decision to stop breaking out its exports to Singapore in financial filings after journalists raised concerns about chip diversion. Members of Congress from both parties say they want answers from Nvidia, with many citing alarm about China and some questioning the White House’s role in Huang’s return. Three committees in the House of Representatives will privately interview Huang and Nvidia’s top lawyer, Tim Teter, next week. Teter reportedly intervened in the Department of Commerce’s investigation of Megaspeed last year. “We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of Nvidia products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities,” the Republican chairs of House committees focused on foreign affairs, intelligence, and China said in a joint statement. Rep. Brian Mast, the chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has also demanded that the Department of Commerce share extensive data regarding its investigation into chip smuggling, including by Megaspeed and its affiliates. The Senate Banking Committee will also question Huang in a public hearing on December 3. “Mr. Huang, Nvidia executives, and the company’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democratic member on the committee, said in a statement. “The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what ‘input’ was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement.” When you purchase through links in our articles,

stories.title: Jensen Huang Apologizes to Nvidia Employees in First All-Hands Since His Return
stories.summary: The Nvidia CEO opened up about his personal life, defended his reinstatement, and acknowledged that his intense management style had hurt his staff.

sources.name: Wired AI
sources.title: Jensen Huang Apologizes to Nvidia Employees in First All-Hands Since His Return
sources.text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told employees on Tuesday that the company’s code of conduct allows room for a “second chance,” that succession planning is a “flawed’ process,” and that he would work to rein in his “insanely intense” management style , according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. During his first all-hands since returning as CEO, Huang acknowledged that he violated the company’s policies and made some “very serious personal mistakes” that damaged his relationships with his wife and two children and prompted him to resign. But he said Nvidia’s board of directors made the appropriate decision for the company in welcoming him back. He added that the board made that call, not “the highest levels of our government.” Huang spoke for about an hour, offering deeply personal thoughts about his therapy sessions and drawing applause at times from employees at Nvidia’s Silicon Valley headquarters as he spoke about the company’s success and future. He didn’t take any questions. While some Nvidia employees celebrated Huang’s return, others remained concerned about his behavior and the board’s decision to reinstate him. “This is going to be the hardest company meeting I’ve ever done, and the second hardest meeting I have ever done,” Huang said as he began to speak. “The hardest meeting I’ve ever done was with my wife.” Nvidia’s board accepted Huang’s resignation earlier this month, citing concerns about his personal behavior and lack of candor following news reports about extramarital affairs, including one with a woman accused of having ties to Chinese intelligence services. The very same board reinstated him on Monday, just 11 days later, after receiving fresh assurances from Huang and learning from the Trump administration that he was not under federal criminal scrutiny and his return would not be a risk to national security. Huang and Nvidia, though, continue to face other legal and regulatory challenges. The board is investigating whether he was the target of foreign intelligence. US lawmakers expect him to testify before Congress next week. Lawsuits and other probes are ongoing into Nvidia’s disclosures about Huang’s behavior and its compliance with US export controls on chips. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Huang told staffers that he has been going to therapy “every day for an hour and a half” and that it’s “been helping me a lot.” He added that he “made some very serious personal mistakes. I hurt my family, I hurt my wife.” While Huang said he had never knowingly made a decision contrary to the company’s interests, he conceded that “in this one area” he had lacked “the courage” to disclose information that he knew would hurt his family, seemingly referring to the extramarital affairs. “The board and I spent the whole weekend together, and they, of course, they've been contemplating, and they've been collecting facts,” Huang said. “They came to the judgment that they would like to invite me back as the CEO, to give me a second chance.” The CEO emphasized that Nvidia’s code of conduct, much of which he said he wrote himself, still governs how employees are expected to treat one another and is intended to “create an environment that’s safe for people.” Huang told employees that violations of the code would not be tolerated. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” he said. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” would factor in. “It has to always be evaluated in the context of the human,” he said. “And this company has been more than gracious, more than thoughtful, more than fair in giving me a second chance.” Huang also pushed back against the notion that he had received preferential treatment because of his status in Silicon Valley. “There are rumors on the internet that apparently I’m a tech bro, and therefore I’m back,” Huang said. He rejected the suggestion that he was above the law or Nvidia’s code of conduct. Later in the meeting, Huang addressed criticism of his self-described “deeply intense, insanely intense” management style, acknowledging that his behavior had at times negatively affected employees. While Huang maintained that the intensity he brings to his job elevates those around him, he conceded that he sometimes takes things too far. “It disempowers them, and that’s not right,” Huang said. The Nvidia CEO said he needed to figure out how to maintain his level of dedication to the company without hurting the people who work there. “I need to hold myself to a higher standard at this time,” Huang said. He said that he would undergo a 360-degree performance review, soliciting feedback as often as monthly from people who work with him. The CEO added that he would be the first and only person at Nvidia to undergo such a review and that he did not want to institute the practice companywide. Huang acknowledged during the meeting that Trump was a vocal supporter of Nvidia but insisted that politics played no role in how the company operated. “It is absolutely true that President Trump really, really loves our company,” Huang said. “He is my president. And I’ll do everything I can to help this president.” Huang said he would take the same approach with future US presidents. “We are the most apolitical company,” he said. “I don’t love that we talk about politics here. I love that we talk about work here.” Huang also sought to reassure women at Nvidia, describing himself as “one of our greatest advocates for creating an environment for women” and touting the company’s flexible work policies, which he said allow employees to simultaneously build their families and careers. “If I did anything that put that in jeopardy, I cannot tell you how sad I am, and I’ll do everything I can to fix it,” Huang said. After Huang’s resignation, he and the company’s board received criticism from Wall Street for not having an obvious internal successor in line. Huang addressed the issue head-on during the company meeting.

sources.title: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it
sources.text: When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired . “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO. It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia. Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct . As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace. “People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.” The consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics. “For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’” Plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.” Of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a company like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession plan, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer. “I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the company are almost impossible to separate,” he said. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.” In that context, Huang’s stutter-step over the code of conduct is easier to understand. Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far. But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the company. sources.name: The Guardian Technology
sources.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologizes to staff: ‘I made some terrible mistakes’
sources.text: Huang acknowledges he violated code of conduct by having affairs, but denied Trump was instrumental in his return Jensen Huang apologized to staff on Tuesday for the tumult he has caused at Nvidia. The company’s CEO acknowledged he violated the code of conduct for having extramarital affairs, but pushed back on the reports that Donald Trump was instrumental in his reinstatement as chief executive. “I made some terrible mistakes,” he said, according to a livestream reviewed by the New York Times . “I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids and, of course, I hurt all of you.” The apology came one day after Huang returned as CEO of Nvidia , and less than two weeks after he was ousted from the role. Following a whiplash series of events, the company’s board of directors reinstated Huang on Monday, despite his admission that he had had an affair. News reports allege the CEO had romantic relationships with two company employees and a suspected Chinese spy. During Tuesday’s apology, Huang told staffers he was in therapy and that it was “not acceptable” that he violated the company’s code of conduct. In an impromptu speech to employees on Monday, Huang said he was “terribly sorry for putting all of you through all of this” and that he was “going to be a better CEO the second time around”. While Huang apologized for his affairs, he rejected narratives that he was a “tech bro” who was “above the law”, according to the New York Times. He added that it was “completely untrue” that Trump pressured Nvidia’s board to reinstate him. The board changed course, he said, because it “evaluated the entire situation” and “gathered facts”. Huang said Trump assured the board that he was not a national security threat. The US government has been investigating whether Megaspeed , a Singapore-based company formerly run by Huang’s alleged ex-lover, Alice Huang (no relation), diverted Nvidia semiconductors to China in breach of export controls. US government officials have also raised concerns about Alice Huang’s alleged role as a Chinese asset. Trump reportedly dialed into Nvidia’s Sunday board meeting to advocate for Huang’s return, according to Semafor . Nvidia’s board publicly said on Monday that it reached its decision to bring back Huang with “input from senior levels of the United States government”. Huang potentially faces two congressional hearings next week, one before the House foreign affairs committee and one before the Senate Banking committee. Gregory Meeks, a Democratic congressman from New York and ranking member of the House foreign affairs committee, said on Tuesday that despite Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia’s CEO, a hearing should still take place. “The American people deserve to hear publicly from Mr Huang about how potentially billions of dollars’ worth of our most advanced technology wound up in the hands of our greatest competitor, and what role this administration played,” Meeks said. Nvidia did not immediately respond to request for comment.

sources.title: Jensen Huang tells staff that Nvidia doesn't need a succession plan
sources.text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Tuesday struck a conciliatory and remorseful tone while leading his first employee meeting since being reinstated, and said how sorry he was for what he had done. Huang told employees that he let them down and promised to do a better job the second time around, according to people inside the room, who asked not to be named in order to share details. "I hurt all of you," Huang said, according to one of the people. The CEO also addressed succession planning during the event, the people said. He told staff that Nvidia has built a team that doesn't require succession planning the way a normal organization does, because the company operates a unique business model where there are multiple capable leaders at Nvidia that are leading different parts of the organization. A succession plan would create unnecessary hierarchy, Huang said, according to one of the people present. Investors and analysts were left to speculate about the company's future leadership in the wake of Huang's resignation on Nov. 12. On Monday, Huang was reinstated as CEO of the chipmaker by Nvidia's board of directors. Eleven days before, Huang had resigned from Nvidia after multiple reported affairs , including one with a Chinese businesswoman who is alleged to be a spy for Beijing. Harvey Jones, Nvidia's newly appointed board chair, said last week that Huang resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms." Huang started the meeting by thanking CFO Colette Kress for her leadership as interim CEO. Huang told staff that Tuesday's company meeting was the second hardest meeting of his life, the first one being with his wife. He said he is in therapy, according to one of the people present. In a press release announcing Huang's return on Monday, the company said the board "received input" from senior officials in the federal government about any potential national security risk around the CEO. President Donald Trump told CNBC that he gave the board assurances and "made the deal" to restore Huang to his post. After the company had its worst week in the stock market since 2008, the stock surged more than 30% the day his return was announced. Shares fell on Tuesday, however. An Nvidia representative didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.
